anchor: GS3.1 Indian economy: resource mobilisation, growth, development, employment
argumentsAgainst: Weekly movements in reserves or deposits should not be treated as a standalone indicator of macroeconomic weakness or strength.
The figures are provisional and differences may arise from rounding; the extract also reflects specified methodological exclusions and merger effects.
argumentsFor: The supplement offers a compact dashboard of external-sector resilience, banking intermediation and monetary conditions.
Disaggregating reserves into foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and IMF reserve position prevents misleading interpretation of total reserves.
Separating demand and time deposits and food and non-food credit helps assess the composition of banking activity.
background: The Reserve Bank of India publishes weekly statistical information covering its liabilities and assets, foreign exchange reserves, scheduled commercial-bank business and monetary aggregates.

M3 is presented through currency with the public, demand deposits with banks, time deposits with banks and other deposits with the Reserve Bank; its sources include net bank credit to government and bank credit to the commercial sector.

Growth in bank credit can support investment and consumption, while the composition between food and non-food credit matters for judging whether financing is reaching productive sectors.
Changes in demand and time deposits can affect banks’ liquidity and funding structure, but the weekly data alone cannot establish a durable credit cycle or financial instability.

example.heading: Hypothetical illustration
example.text: If an economy records stable total reserves but a changing mix of foreign currency assets and gold, an analyst should examine the composition and valuation effects before concluding that external resilience has changed. Similarly, faster bank credit growth should be read with deposit and sectoral-credit composition rather than treated as proof of broad-based investment.

pocketRead.excerpt: The RBI’s weekly supplement links reserve composition with deposits, credit and M3, but provisional weekly movements require cautious interpretation.

question.answer: Use the supplement as a dashboard rather than a verdict: examine the direction and composition of reserves, deposits and credit; then test any inference against inflation, external liabilities, fiscal conditions and financial-stability indicators. A single weekly change cannot establish a durable trend or causality.
question.prompt: How should a policymaker interpret a weekly RBI statistical supplement without overreading its figures?

sections.heading: RBI’s weekly dashboard
paragraphs: On 6 November 2026, the Reserve Bank of India published a weekly statistical supplement reporting reserve, banking and monetary data. The extract records total foreign exchange reserves of 717056 US$ Mn as on 30 October 2026, alongside their four reported components.

The same release reports scheduled commercial-bank deposits and credit as on 15 October 2026, and M3 with its components and sources. This places external liquidity and domestic monetary conditions in one statistical frame.

sections.heading: Composition limits interpretation
paragraphs: A total-reserves figure does not by itself reveal the source or quality of the buffer: the supplement separately reports foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and the reserve position in the IMF, with exclusions for foreign currency assets. Bank-credit totals likewise require attention to food and non-food credit.

The data are provisional, and the extract notes rounding differences. Merger effects are also included in the banking series. Therefore, a weekly movement is a monitoring signal, not conclusive evidence of a structural change.

M3 is presented through currency with the public, demand deposits with banks, time deposits with banks and other deposits with the Reserve Bank.
use: Use the supplement to answer questions on RBI monetary surveillance, reserve composition, banking liquidity, money supply and the interpretation of high-frequency economic indicators.

advisory_notes: The proposed publication time is more precise than the extract supports; use the document’s stated date, 6 November 2026.
The static definition of M3 accurately follows the components shown, but its broader monetary interpretation should be presented as explanatory analysis.
The reserve-adequacy discussion is sound analysis, but import needs, external liabilities and exchange rates are not supplied by this extract.
The headline and deck appropriately describe composition and caution, though “links” may imply a relationship the release itself does not establish.
The hypothetical example is clearly labelled and logically sound, but valuation effects are an analytical possibility rather than a finding in this release.
The applied-question answer is substantively appropriate, while “policy response” in the diagram is a broad analytical extension beyond the reported statistics.
The GS3.1 anchor is relevant to monetary, banking and macroeconomic analysis; GS3.2 and GS3.3 are plausible extensions but may be less direct than GS3.1.

wayForward: Read weekly figures with longer time series and cross-check them against inflation, exchange-rate, external-liability, fiscal and financial-stability indicators.
Separate level, percentage change and composition before drawing conclusions about liquidity or credit conditions.
Preserve transparency about provisional status, rounding, merger effects and the stated exclusions from foreign currency assets.
Use sectoral credit and deposit trends to assess transmission and inclusion, while avoiding causal claims unsupported by the data.
